tools.title: The NVIDIA story is a BFD
tools.summary_raw: 13 slightly speculative takes on the political fallout
tools.content_text: Getty Images/Silver Bulletin illustration. Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, one of the world’s most valuable companies and perhaps the most strategically important corporation to the future of the United States, resigned after admitting to an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe was a Chinese spy. This is a big fucking deal. Thanks, Captain Obvious. But my impression is that the political world is under-reacting to the Nvidia story. We’re overdue to have at least an initial newsletter covering it. I don’t expect this to become a Silver Bulletin obsession, but the overlap between politics and AI is well within our purview, and this story falls within those sightlines. I’m going to do this as one of those “13 thoughts” bullet-pointed lists that can make for a nice shortcut for these developing news stories. The usual ground rule is that I’m working through my thinking with you in real time, so treat this as provisional. To be clear, this is political analysis, not a scandal explainer. For more about the scandal itself, read Zvi or listen to these recent editions of Odd Lots or Search Engine: Basically, what those describe is that this story isn’t just about Jensen Huang having slept with an alleged Chinese agent, Alice Huang. As this New York Times graphic illustrates , there’s also a broader penumbra of suspicion related to a company called Megaspeed, which Alice Huang ran and which bought Nvidia chips through Nvidia’s hardware partners. U.S. authorities began investigating Megaspeed in 2024, during the Biden administration, over whether it diverted advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The Commerce Department’s work on the probe was paused in late 2025, and the case was “abruptly transferred” to the Justice Department, the Times reported . My 13 thoughts A canonically good bet is to “buy the rumor but sell the news.” In other words, to bet on people overreacting. That would have been good advice in the case of Haley Stevens’s endorsement of Mike Rogers , for instance. But I think there’s a case for buying the news when the news cycle is particularly busy . The political news world has been knee-deep in the midterms, which is an absolutely massive story given the magnitude of the Democratic sweep. I don’t think it’s an exaggeration to say it’s one of the bigger political earthquakes of the century . However, public attention spans and journalistic bandwidth are finite resources. The timing might lead one to downplay the magnitude of the Nvidia story. It will probably build. In terms of the magnitude, the comparison that comes to mind is the onset of the Iran War, which also dropped amid a busy news cycle 1 . Nvidia is not the same sort of story, but it is of roughly the same shape and size , because there are tripartite implications for the economy, for geopolitics and for domestic politics. Read more

market.title: France’s Actu changed its business model and got free readers to pay
market.summary_raw: Actu.fr is one of France’s largest websites. It’s built on content from more than 100 local and regional newsrooms. Until recently, its digital output was free and ad supported. During the past couple years, Actu moved to a mix of paid and free content, and it's gaining around 1,500 new subscribers a month.
market.content_text: In the past, Actu, owned by CIPA Ouest-France, had 400 journalists producing some 80 weekly print editions, mostly in Brittany and Normandy in northwestern France. These print titles each had their own websites. They later shifted to a single platform for digital content, which offered national reach. “From that, we decided to pivot to a paid model, which was quite a big challenge for us,” Amandine Briand , Deputy Director, Editorial Projects at Groupe Actu, told our Digital Media Europe participants in London. The roots of their current efforts began in 2012, when the group decided to launch a digital-only edition, 76Actu, to see what would happen, she said. The site quickly proved popular and gained a large audience, so the group launched Actu Toulouse, also digital only in 2015, Briand said. WAN-IFRA Members can download Briand’s presentation slides as well as replay this session and others from Digital Media Europe on our Knowledge Hub. A national footprint based on local news However, the group still had many websites connected to their weekly print titles operating independently, some of which had only 2,000 or so unique visitors a month. “We thought it would be a good idea to put everyone on the same platform and get these audiences growing, which is what we did in 2016, and got 80 titles on the same domain,” Briand said. By doing that, she said, traffic skyrocketed. “We now reach around 115 million monthly users, and we are one of France’s most visited websites.” This gave them a national footprint, even though they provide local news. “But unlike traditional media, we really operate as a network,” Briand added. “We don’t have a top-down approach, more a bottom-up one.” Everything was working quite well: “audiences exploded and the traffic was good. The advertising was fine,” Briand said. However as market dynamics began to shift as they did for so many news publishers worldwide during the past decade, the group realised it needed to change, too. “We decided we could no longer just count on advertising, and on revenues that are mainly dependencies, so we decided to do this shift,” she said. ‘Will this monetisation project kill the audience?’ Actu had three major goals as they started the project, Briand said. Reduce dependencies Transform their economic model Put content at the centre The third goal was the most ambitious of the three, she noted. The project itself raised many questions and some fears within Actu’s newsrooms. One major concern, Briand said, was “will this monetisation project actually kill the audience?” They had spent years building up their audiences, and worried the move to charging readers could “just crush everything,” she said. After all, Actu had spent years giving readers free content online, and now they were going to ask those readers to pay. Additionally, there was a concern that maybe they were making the move too late. […]

market.content_text: It’s been another busy week. Recap it with the second edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading . The quiz will appear here through November as a trial run; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027.
